pinboard.title: GM to pay $220m to settle allegations it violated drivers' privacy • Reuters
pinboard.description:
Jonathan Stempel:

General Motors will pay $220m to settle ​allegations that it illegally sold drivers' private behavior and location data to ‌brokers, who then sold the information to insurers that used it to set and sometimes increase rates. The settlement, announced on Thursday, resolves claims by the attorneys general of 35 US states and the District ​of Columbia over the automaker's Smart Driver program, which enrolled millions of drivers ​between 2016 and its discontinuation in 2024. Other regulators have also reviewed ⁠GM's handling of driver data. GM was accused of pitching Smart Driver to help ​people improve their personal driving safety, only to violate drivers' privacy by reneging on its ​promise not to sell their data without permission. Many people who signed up were also enrolled in GM's OnStar safety, navigation and diagnostic service. "People bought a car, not a tracking device," Oregon Attorney General ​Dan Rayfield said in a statement. Rayfield's office and the office of Washington Attorney ​General Nick Brown led the bipartisan state coalition. The settlement also requires GM to limit driving data it ‌collects, ⁠and obtain drivers' express consent before collecting or sharing that data. A GM spokesperson said the settlement reinforces other steps the Detroit automaker has taken to strengthen privacy.

It's just astonishing how companies can straight-out lie like this. GM had revenue of $167bn, operating profits of $11bn in 2025; after restructuring charges, still $3.1bn. So this is the tiniest of scratches. But equally, they couldn't have made any appreciable money from selling the data. Just ruined the brand.

pinboard.title: Patrick Stewart: the legacy of domestic violence | Domestic violence | The Guardian
pinboard.description:
My father was, in many ways, a man of discipline, organisation and charisma - a regimental sergeant major no less. One of the very last men to be evacuated from Dunkirk, his third stripe was chalked on to his uniform by an officer when no more senior NCOs were left alive. Parachuted into Crete and Italy, both times under fire, he fought at Monte Casino and was twice mentioned in dispatches. A fellow soldier once told me, "When your father marches on to the parade ground, the birds in the trees stop singing."

In civilian life it was a different story. He was an angry, unhappy and frustrated man who was not able to control his emotions or his hands. As a child I witnessed his repeated violence against my mother, and the terror and misery he caused was such that, if I felt I could have succeeded, I would have killed him. If my mother had attempted it, I would have held him down. For those who struggle to comprehend these feelings in a child, imagine living in an environment of emotional unpredictability, danger and humiliation week after week, year after year, from the age of seven. My childish instinct was to protect my mother, but the man hurting her was my father, whom I respected, admired and feared.
pinboard.byline_hint: Pinboard Popular · tagged: guardian, patrickstewart, writing, domesticviolence
